The Grey-crowned babbler Pomatostomus temporalis is a cooperatively breeding passerine endemic to Australia and southern New Guinea. Standard incubation temperatures in the nest, recorded via data loggers placed within the domed structure, average 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the incubation period lasts 23 days [ab = 23 days], a duration consistent with that of other pomatostomid babblers of similar body mass at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Upon hatching, altricial nestlings emerge with a wet weight of 3.85 grams [Wwb = 3.85 grams], a relatively low neonatal mass characteristic of species that exhibit extended post-hatching parental care. The rapid growth phase during the early nestling period is supported by intensive provisioning from both the breeding pair and auxiliary helpers drawn from previous broods.

Physiological development in the nest proceeds under a thermal regime that frequently reaches 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during peak diurnal activity in the canopy, a temperature that corresponds to the typical body temperature of an active adult. Fledging occurs 20 days after hatching [tx = 20 days after hatching], marking the point at which young birds achieve their first sustained flight and depart the nest at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is comparable to values reported for other medium-sized insectivorous passerines. The fledglings remain dependent on the family group for several weeks after nest departure, gradually acquiring foraging skills through observational learning and food-begging interactions with adult helpers.

Sexual maturity in this species is attained at 60 days since birth [tp = 60 days since birth], a rapid maturation schedule that facilitates the early recruitment of helpers into the cooperative breeding system at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Under the same thermal conditions typical of the active foraging period at 41.6 °C, individuals begin their first reproductive attempt at 365 days after birth [tR = 365 days after birth] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay between physiological puberty and first breeding reflects the time required to establish a territory, form a dominance hierarchy within the group, and secure a breeding position. Many young birds therefore serve as helpers at the nest for one or more seasons before they themselves initiate a clutch.

Adult body mass data, compiled from multiple field studies across northern Australia, show that fully grown Grey-crowned babblers reach an ultimate wet weight of 75 grams [Wwi = 75 grams]. Published records indicate that individual adult mass varies considerably, spanning a range from 62 to 83 grams, with seasonal fluctuations linked to food availability and reproductive status. The cooperative social system and the presence of helpers are thought to buffer against energetic shortfalls during provisioning periods. Under the elevated metabolic conditions associated with 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum recorded longevity in the wild is 15 years [am = 15 years], placing this species among the longer-lived passerines for its body size.

Reproductive output in the Grey-crowned babbler is characterized by a maximum of two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], with each clutch containing 3 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 3 eggs]. These values, recorded at a typical nest microclimate of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], represent the upper bound of the species' reproductive potential under favorable environmental conditions. The cooperative breeding system likely enables this moderate reproductive rate by distributing the costs of incubation and provisioning among multiple group members. Population-level surveys indicate that within stable groups, only one pair per social unit typically breeds, while other group members act as non-breeding helpers that improve overall nesting success and post-fledging survival. Among the family Pomatostomidae, which comprises medium-sized Australo-Papuan babblers, the Grey-crowned babbler's combination of a 15-year maximum lifespan (15 years) [am = 15 years] and a maximum of two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year] with three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = three eggs per clutch] aligns with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and cooperative care over high fecundity at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This strategy is considered adaptive in the species' unpredictable, fire-prone habitats, where helper-assisted reproduction buffers the costs of prolonged parental investment and promotes stability in group dynamics across successive breeding seasons.
